title: Swedish Meatballs EVERYONE's Grandma Made (Why Yours Turn Out HARD)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, in nineteen sixty-seven, every party in America had a little pot of Swedish meatballs keeping warm on a table, with a basket of toothpicks next to it. Little round meatballs in a creamy brown gravy, with a whisper of nutmeg. People stood around that pot all night, spearing them one at a time and telling themselves just one more. I never saw that pot go home with anything in it.
scenes.caption: JUST ONE MORE

scenes.text: But people tell me their meatballs come out hard as golf balls, or dry inside, or the gravy is thin and gray and lumpy. So tonight I'm giving you Mrs. Lindqvist's Swedish meatballs, a real family supper, every step, and the five mistakes that make them hard. And stay with me, because the last secret is in the gravy, and it's a jar most of us have in the icebox door.
scenes.caption: HARD AS GOLF BALLS

scenes.text: Mrs. Lindqvist, the Swedish widow from our church in Mansfield, made them every Sunday. In Swedish they're called kottbullar, and every grandmother in Sweden has her own recipe. Hers were small, about the size of a walnut, soft as a pillow, and served with mashed potatoes, the brown cream gravy, and a spoon of lingonberry jam on the side. I'd never seen jam with meat. I thought she'd lost her mind.
scenes.caption: JAM WITH MEAT?

scenes.text: Then I tasted it, honey. The sweet, tart berries with the rich, salty gravy and the soft meatball. It was the best bite I'd had in my whole life, at fourteen years old. I went home and asked my mother to put grape jelly on our pot roast. She said no, very firmly. In a minute I'll tell you why Mrs. Lindqvist's meatballs were so soft, and it's something from your bread box.
scenes.caption: THE BEST BITE

scenes.text: And they're cheap, sweetheart. A pound and a half of meat makes about forty little meatballs, enough for six people with potatoes. The whole supper costs about fourteen dollars. And they freeze beautifully, so you can make a double batch on a Sunday afternoon and have supper ready for two busy weeknights later.
scenes.caption: ABOUT FOURTEEN DOLLARS

scenes.text: Here's what you need, honey. One pound of ground beef and half a pound of ground pork. Half a small onion, grated. Two slices of white bread, crusts off, torn up. A third of a cup of milk. One egg. One teaspoon of salt, half a teaspoon of pepper, and a quarter teaspoon each of nutmeg and allspice. Those two spices are what make them taste Swedish.
scenes.query: ground beef pork bread milk spices
scenes.caption: NUTMEG AND ALLSPICE

scenes.text: For the gravy. Three tablespoons of butter. Three tablespoons of flour. Two cups of beef broth. Three quarters of a cup of heavy cream or sour cream. A tablespoon of soy sauce or Worcestershire. And the secret ingredient, from the icebox door, which I'll tell you about at the end. For serving, mashed potatoes or egg noodles, and lingonberry or cranberry sauce.
scenes.caption: THE GRAVY

scenes.text: Step one, and here's the secret from the bread box. Put the torn bread in a big bowl, pour the milk over it, and let it sit for five minutes, until it's soft and mushy. Then mash it with a fork. That's called a panade, honey. Mistake number one is using dry bread crumbs, or no bread at all. The milky bread is what keeps the meatballs soft and juicy inside.
scenes.caption: FROM THE BREAD BOX

scenes.text: And grate the onion, don't chop it. Use the big holes of a box grater. Mistake number two is big chunks of raw onion. They don't cook through in a small meatball, and they make the meatballs fall apart. Grated onion melts right into the meat and keeps it moist. Mrs. Lindqvist cooked her grated onion in a little butter first, so it was sweet. I do too.
scenes.caption: GRATE THE ONION

scenes.text: Step two. Add the meat, the onion, the egg, the salt, pepper, nutmeg and allspice to the soaked bread. And now mistake number three. Mixing it too hard. If you squeeze and knead the meat like bread dough, the meatballs turn dense and tough. Mix it gently with your fingertips, or a fork, just until everything is together. Stop the minute it looks even.
scenes.caption: MIX IT GENTLY

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. Now wet your hands with cold water, so the meat doesn't stick, and roll the meatballs about an inch across, the size of a walnut. Keep them all the same size, so they cook evenly. Set them on a tray. If you have time, chill them for thirty minutes, so they hold their shape in the pan.
scenes.caption: THE SIZE OF A WALNUT

scenes.text: Mrs. Lindqvist could roll forty meatballs in about six minutes, perfectly round, while talking the whole time about the pastor's sermon. I timed her once. It takes me fifteen, and mine aren't as round. She said, Ruth, roll them lightly, like you're holding a baby bird. Squeeze them, and they'll be tough. I still hear her voice every time I make them.
scenes.caption: LIKE A BABY BIRD

scenes.text: Step three. Melt a tablespoon of butter with a tablespoon of oil in a big skillet over medium heat. Add the meatballs in one layer, with room between them. Mistake number four is crowding the pan. Too many at once, and they steam instead of browning, and they turn gray. Cook them in batches, turning them gently, until they're brown all over, about eight to ten minutes.
scenes.caption: DON'T CROWD THE PAN

scenes.text: Shake the pan instead of turning each one with a fork, honey. They roll around and brown on all sides, and they stay round. Take them out onto a plate when they're brown. They don't have to be cooked all the way through yet, because they'll finish in the gravy. And don't wash that pan. All those brown bits are the start of the gravy.
scenes.caption: SHAKE THE PAN

scenes.text: Step four, the gravy. In the same pan, melt three tablespoons of butter. Whisk in the flour and cook it, stirring, for two or three minutes, until it turns a light brown, like peanut butter. Then slowly whisk in the beef broth, scraping up all the brown bits from the bottom. Let it bubble until it thickens, about three minutes. Then stir in the cream and the soy sauce.
scenes.caption: LIKE PEANUT BUTTER

scenes.text: And mistake number five, the lumpy gray gravy. It comes from pouring all the broth in at once into raw flour. Cook the flour first, until it's golden, so it tastes toasty, not pasty. And pour the broth in slowly, a little at a time, whisking hard. If you get lumps anyway, pour it through a strainer, or whisk like your life depends on it. Mrs. Lindqvist never had a lump in her life.
scenes.caption: NOT A LUMP

scenes.text: Now put the meatballs back in the gravy, cover the pan, and let them simmer gently for about ten minutes, until they're cooked all the way through. Spoon the gravy over them now and then. Taste the gravy and add salt and pepper. It should be smooth, creamy and light brown, the color of coffee with plenty of cream in it.
scenes.caption: COFFEE WITH CREAM

scenes.text: So far, bread soaked in milk, grated onion, a gentle mix, small even meatballs, browned in batches, and a toasty gravy. And now Mrs. Lindqvist's last secret, from the icebox door. Right before serving, stir a big spoonful of lingonberry jam, or red currant jelly, or cranberry sauce, into the gravy itself. Just one tablespoon. It doesn't make it sweet, honey. It makes it taste finished, round and rich.
scenes.caption: FROM THE ICEBOX DOOR
scenes.chapter: The secret in the icebox door

scenes.text: And that's why she served the jam on the side, too. Sweet and tart with salty and creamy. You can find lingonberry jam at most big grocery stores now, or at that Swedish furniture store with the cafeteria. But plain cranberry sauce from the can works just fine. I use whatever's left over from Thanksgiving. My husband finally admitted she hadn't lost her mind after all.
scenes.caption: SHE HADN'T LOST HER MIND

scenes.text: Serve them over a big pile of mashed potatoes or buttered egg noodles, with plenty of gravy, a spoon of berries on the side, and a little chopped parsley or dill on top. And Mrs. Lindqvist always served quick pickled cucumbers on the side, sliced thin in vinegar, sugar and dill. They're cool and crisp next to the warm, rich gravy.
scenes.caption: THE SWEDISH WAY

scenes.text: And for a party, honey, do it the nineteen sixty-seven way. Make them a little smaller, keep them warm in a slow cooker in the gravy, and put a cup of toothpicks next to it. And to freeze them, cook the meatballs and the gravy, cool them, and freeze them together in containers for three months. Thaw them overnight and warm them gently on the stove.
scenes.caption: THE 1967 WAY

scenes.text: So one more time. Soak white bread in milk. Grate the onion. Beef and pork, nutmeg and allspice. Mix it gently, roll them like a baby bird. Brown them in batches. Cook the flour golden, and whisk the broth in slowly. Cream, and a spoon of jam in the gravy. That's Mrs. Lindqvist's Swedish meatballs, soft as a pillow and never hard.
scenes.caption: SOFT AS A PILLOW

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Jam with meatballs, yes or no? I know some of you think we're crazy. The whole playlist of Grandma's recipes is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey.
scenes.caption: JAM, YES OR NO?
